title: MeshFIM: Local Low-Poly Mesh Editing via Fill-in-the-Middle Autoregressive Generation
claim: Local regions with missing or crude structure can be regenerated from reference and context, blending seamlessly with the surrounding existing structure.
layout: 2x2 grid of example groups, left-to-right rows, color-coded selection regions
description: A gallery of four example groups, split into Refinement (top) and Repair (bottom) bands by a dashed divider. Each group has two rows. The top row goes from a high-poly ground-truth reference object, to a zoomed clay-rendered close-up, to the regenerated wireframe result. The bottom row goes from the low-poly input object, to a zoomed local selection with the target region in blue and context in orange, to a version with the region deleted, shown as a dark gap. Small up-arrows link the gapped mesh to the final result. Teal arrows show the flow. Results show clean quad or triangle meshes with blue regenerated patches that join the orange context. Labels read 'GT (High Poly) Reference', 'Low-Poly Input', 'Local Selection' and 'Results'. The eye goes first to the colorful wireframe close-ups.
caption: MeshFIM enables accurate local low-poly mesh editing. Given an input low-poly mesh, a target local region (blue) is selected via flexible interactive tools (e.g. sec.5.1) or automatic defect detection algorithms (e.g. sec.5.2). Conditioned on ground truth reference high poly and context mesh (orange), MeshFIM regenerates the target region for refinement (top) or repair (bottom) while preserving seamless boundary connectivity and smooth edge flow with surrounding existing mesh.
abstract: Autoregressive (AR) models can generate high-quality low-poly meshes from point clouds, but they still operate in an all-or-nothing manner: when a local region is unsatisfactory, the entire mesh must be regenerated, wasting computation and destroying satisfactory mesh structure elsewhere. We introduce MeshFIM, a Fill-in-the-Middle (FIM) framework that regenerates a target region of a low-poly mesh conditioned on the surrounding context. MeshFIM addresses three mesh-specific challenges: enforcing exact attachment along the exposed boundary, preserving topological order in the context, and suppressing overflow beyond the intended region. It does so with five complementary design choices: boundary vertex markers, context positional embeddings, expanded context width, context augmentation, and a low-poly geometry encoder whose gated subtraction mechanism focuses generation on the missing region by leveraging the difference between the reference surface and the existing mesh. Detailed ablation studies are presented to show the effectiveness of every introduced component. Based on MeshFIM, we demonstrate two applications: interactive brush-based editing and automatic defect repair on low-poly mesh (see Figure 1). Last but not least, experiments show that MeshFIM outperforms a range of baselines in mesh refinement, mesh repair and whole mesh generation plus stitch-back scheme.
